content: It has been proposed that deficiencies in omega-3 fatty acids may contribute to the impairments observed in individuals with autism spectrum disorders (ASD). Supplementation with these essential fatty acids has been hypothesized to potentially improve symptoms associated with ASD. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of omega-3 fatty acid supplementation in improving core features of ASD, such as social interaction, communication, and repetitive behaviors (stereotypies), as well as associated symptoms like hyperactivity. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was performed on June 2, 2010. These databases included CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, BIOSIS, CINAHL, Science Citation Index, Social Science Citation Index, metaRegister of Controlled Trials, and ClinicalTrials.gov. Additionally, Dissertation Abstracts International was searched in 2008, but access to this resource was no longer available by 2010. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared omega-3 fatty acid supplementation to a placebo in individuals diagnosed with ASD. Three independent authors were responsible for selecting studies, assessing their risk of bias, and extracting relevant data. A meta-analysis was conducted on the included studies, focusing on three primary outcomes—social interaction, communication, and stereotypy—and one secondary outcome, hyperactivity. Ultimately, two trials involving a total of 37 children with ASD met the inclusion criteria. These children were randomized to receive either omega-3 fatty acid supplementation or a placebo. Six other trials were excluded because they were either not randomized controlled trials, lacked a control group, or had a control group that did not receive a placebo. The results of the meta-analysis showed no evidence that omega-3 fatty acid supplementation had a significant effect on any of the primary or secondary outcomes. Specifically, there was no improvement in social interaction (mean difference [MD] 0.82, 95% confidence interval [CI] -2.84 to 4.48, I² = 0%), communication (MD 0.62, 95% CI -0.89 to 2.14, I² = 0%), stereotypy (MD 0.77, 95% CI -0.69 to 2.22, I² = 8%), or hyperactivity (MD 3.46, 95% CI -0.79 to 7.70, I² = 0%). The authors concluded that, as of the date of this review, there is no high-quality evidence to support the effectiveness of omega-3 fatty acid supplementation in improving core or associated symptoms of ASD. They emphasized the need for larger, well-designed randomized controlled trials that include both highand low-functioning individuals with ASD and incorporate longer follow-up periods to better assess the potential benefits of omega-3 fatty acids in this population.
